title: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
summary: Describes an updated version of the Encapsulating Security Payload, which provides a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6. These include confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, anti-replay protection, and limited traffic flow confidentiality. It replaces RFC 2406 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A sealed, opaque envelope around your data. Nobody can read it or swap its contents, and old copies are spotted if someone tries to resend them.

subtitle: The IPsec packet wrapper that encrypts and authenticates IP traffic, and spots replayed packets.

tldr.problem: Plain IP packets can be read, altered and replayed by anyone along the path, and hosts or gateways need a standard way to protect them.
tldr.mechanism: ESP wraps the payload in a header (SPI and sequence number) and a trailer (padding, pad length, next header), encrypts the payload and adds an Integrity Check Value so the receiver can verify the packet and reject duplicates.
tldr.outcome: ESP offers confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, anti-replay protection and limited traffic flow confidentiality. This version obsoletes RFC 2406.

facts.label: Extended sequence number
facts.value: 64 bits, with only the low 32 bits sent

today: RFC 4303 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2406. According to the metadata, no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What ESP Provides
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) is designed to provide a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6. It can be applied alone, together with the IP Authentication Header (AH), or nested, and it can protect traffic between two hosts, two security gateways, or a gateway and a host. The RFC assumes the reader knows the Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol (RFC 4301), including Security Associations (SAs).

ESP can provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, an anti-replay service (a form of partial sequence integrity) and limited traffic flow confidentiality. Which ones apply depends on the choices made when the SA is established. The RFC treats data origin authentication and connectionless integrity as joint services called simply integrity.

Three service combinations exist: confidentiality-only (MAY be supported), integrity-only (MUST be supported) and confidentiality plus integrity (MUST be supported). Encryption without strong integrity may be insecure against some active attacks, which is why the RFC warns that encryption-only gives defense mainly against passive attackers. The anti-replay service may be selected only when integrity is selected.
sections.eli5: ESP is like a security guard for your mail. It can hide what is inside, prove nobody changed it, and notice if someone sends the same letter twice. The best setup does all of these together.

sections.title: The ESP Packet Format
sections.content:
The IP header just before ESP carries protocol number 50 (the Protocol field in IPv4 or the Next Header field in IPv6). The ESP packet starts with two 4-byte fields, the Security Parameters Index (SPI) and the Sequence Number. These are followed by the Payload Data, then Padding, the one-byte Pad Length and Next Header fields, and the optional Integrity Check Value (ICV).

The SPI is an arbitrary 32-bit value the receiver uses to find the SA for an incoming packet. Values 1 through 255 are reserved by IANA, and zero is reserved for local use and MUST NOT be sent on the wire. The Sequence Number is a counter that increases by one for each packet sent. The first packet on an SA carries 1, and the sender MUST always include the field, even if the receiver does not check it.

The Payload Data holds the protected content, plus any initialization vector the encryption algorithm needs. Padding (0 to 255 bytes) fills the plaintext to the algorithm's block size and keeps the ICV aligned on a 4-byte boundary. If the encryption algorithm does not specify the padding contents, the default padding bytes count up as 1, 2, 3 and so on, and the receiver SHOULD check them. The Next Header field says what the payload contains, using IP protocol numbers.

ESP has no version number. If backward compatibility is a concern, the peers must use a signaling mechanism such as IKEv2 or out-of-band configuration.
sections.eli5: Picture a package with a label on the front (who it is for and a ticket number), the secret contents, some bubble wrap so it fits the box, a note saying what kind of thing is inside, and a tamper seal at the end.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
ESP can be used in two ways. In transport mode, the ESP header is inserted after the IP header (and any IPv4 options) and before the next layer protocol such as TCP, UDP or ICMP, so only the upper-layer data is protected. In IPv6, ESP is treated as an end-to-end payload and appears after the hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers.

In tunnel mode, the whole original IP packet, header included, becomes the protected payload, and a new outer IP header carries the addresses of the IPsec peers, such as two security gateways. The inner header holds the ultimate source and destination. Mixed inner and outer IP versions are allowed, so IPv6 can travel over IPv4 and the reverse.

In both modes, the encryption covers the payload and the trailer, while the integrity check also covers the ESP header. The name transport mode should not be read as limiting use to TCP and UDP.
sections.eli5: Transport mode seals just the letter inside and leaves the original envelope visible. Tunnel mode puts the whole envelope, address and all, inside a new bigger envelope with a different address.

sections.title: Algorithms and Combined Mode
sections.content:
The mandatory-to-implement algorithms are specified in a separate RFC (RFC 4305), so they can be updated without changing the protocol. Additional algorithms MAY be supported. Confidentiality and integrity are each optional, but at least one MUST be selected, so the encryption and integrity algorithms must not both be NULL.

The encryption algorithm and the integrity algorithm are named by the SA. Each must cope with packets arriving out of order or going missing, so each packet carries the data needed for the receiver to decrypt it, for example an explicit initialization vector in the Payload Data.

Some algorithm modes do encryption and integrity in a single operation. The RFC calls these combined mode algorithms. For them, ESP defines no payload substructure, and the ICV field may be omitted if the algorithm carries its own integrity data. The RFC that defines such an algorithm for ESP must say where the integrity data goes and how the SPI and sequence number are covered.
sections.eli5: ESP does not pick the secret code itself. It just has slots for a scrambler and a seal. Some tools do both jobs at once, and ESP is fine with that.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Packets
sections.content:
To send, the implementation first checks that the packet belongs to an SA calling for ESP. With separate algorithms, the sender puts the next layer data (transport mode) or the entire original IP packet (tunnel mode) into the payload, adds optional TFC padding and encryption padding, encrypts, and then computes the ICV over the ESP packet minus the ICV field. Encryption comes first, so the receiver can reject replayed or bogus packets before decrypting them, which limits denial of service damage, and it also allows decryption and integrity checking in parallel.

To receive, the packet is first matched to an SA using the SPI (plus destination, and possibly source address, for multicast). With no valid SA, the receiver MUST discard the packet, and this is an auditable event. If the ICV does not match, the datagram is discarded as invalid. After decryption, the receiver removes padding, and if the Next Header value is 59 (no next header) the packet is a dummy and is discarded.

Fragmentation is performed after ESP processing, so transport mode ESP is applied only to whole IP datagrams. A receiver that sees what looks like an IP fragment at ESP MUST discard it. An implementation MAY choose not to support fragmentation and mark packets with the DF bit, and it MUST support generation of ICMP PMTU messages to minimize fragmentation.
sections.eli5: The sender wraps and seals the data, then stamps it with a number. The receiver first checks the number and the seal, throws away anything fake or odd, and only then opens the package.

sections.title: Anti-Replay and Extended Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
All ESP implementations MUST support the anti-replay service, though the receiver may enable or disable it per SA. It MUST NOT be enabled unless integrity is also enabled, because otherwise the sequence number is not protected. The sender assumes anti-replay is on and must never let its counter cycle: a new SA, with a new key, MUST be established before the 2^32nd packet. If the key is distributed manually, an implementation SHOULD NOT provide anti-replay.

Duplicates are rejected using a sliding receive window. The right edge is the highest validated sequence number, and packets lower than the left edge are rejected. A minimum window of 32 packets MUST be supported for 32-bit numbers, and 64 is preferred and SHOULD be the default. The window is updated only after integrity verification succeeds. ESP also allows a quick preliminary check before any cryptography, which is useful when the cryptographic hardware cannot keep up with the line rate.

For high-speed links, Extended Sequence Numbers (ESN) SHOULD be implemented. They give a 64-bit counter per SA, but only the low-order 32 bits are sent in each packet. The high-order bits are tracked by both sides and included in the ICV computation. Using ESN MUST be negotiated by an SA management protocol, and in IKEv2 ESN is the default unless 32-bit numbers are negotiated. A receiver that does not use anti-replay SHOULD NOT negotiate ESN.
sections.eli5: Every package gets a ticket number. The receiver keeps a short list of recent numbers and throws away repeats or very old ones. Longer ticket numbers mean the counter does not run out on very fast connections.

sections.title: Auditing and Conformance
sections.content:
Systems that support auditing MUST let an administrator enable or disable auditing for ESP. The RFC names five auditable events: no valid SA exists, a packet looks like an IP fragment, a send would overflow the sequence number, a packet fails the anti-replay checks, and an integrity check fails. Each event SHOULD be logged with details such as the SPI value, the time, the source and destination addresses and the sequence number. The receiver is not required to send a message back to the apparent sender, because that could be used to cause denial of service.

An implementation claiming conformance MUST implement the ESP syntax and processing for unicast traffic and the additional requirements of the Security Architecture, plus the multicast requirements if it supports multicast. NULL encryption support is required, and an implementation offering confidentiality-only MUST also support the NULL integrity algorithm. Integrity and encryption MUST NOT both be NULL.

The security considerations section is brief. It says security is central to the design and permeates the specification, and it points to the Security Architecture for more.
sections.eli5: If something odd happens, such as a package with no matching sender or a broken seal, the receiver writes it in a logbook. It does not shout back at the sender, since a fake sender could use that to cause trouble.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2406
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 2406. Confidentiality-only service is now a MAY instead of a MUST. The SPI lookup is specified as one uniform algorithm for unicast and multicast SAs. New features include the 64-bit Extended Sequence Number, support for combined mode algorithms, extra padding after the end of the IP payload for better traffic flow confidentiality, and dummy packets marked with Next Header 59. The mandatory algorithms moved to a separate document.

On compatibility, if none of the new features are used, an ESP packet is identical in version 2 and version 3. Combined mode algorithms are defined only for version 3, so a version 2 peer would never negotiate one. The extra TFC padding and the dummy packet convention can be used by a sender whether the receiver implements version 2 or 3, though the RFC says it is an open question how a version 2 receiver handles Next Header 59, and that it ought not to crash.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. Most of the old rules still work, and the new tricks are optional extras that older systems can safely ignore.
